CLOSED 2026-11-24. NO DEFECT. The bead's premise does not apply, for a structural reason, and the mitigation that makes the design coherent is real and already tested.

## Why the IP-literal bypass cannot exist here

pkix-aia-http's bug was that reqwest does not consult a custom DNS resolver for an IP literal, so its RESOLUTION-TIME destination filter was bypassed.

pkix-revocation-http has no destination filter, at any layer, sync or async. That is explicit and documented, not an oversight -- lib.rs states: "No CDP / AIA URI filtering. This crate fetches whichever URI is in the certificate's CRLDistributionPoints or AuthorityInfoAccess extension. Restrictions on which hosts / schemes are acceptable for revocation fetches (e.g., enforcing HTTPS or blocking private-network URIs) are a deployment-policy decision and stay outside this crate."

No filter means nothing to bypass. The bug class simply does not arise.

## The mitigation that makes that decision coherent, verified

Leaving destination policy to the caller only works if the caller's vetting cannot be subverted after the fact. The crate claims exactly that: "The reference clients only follow same-origin redirects by default, so a vetted URL cannot be redirected to a different host behind the caller's back."

That claim is true and tested on BOTH paths, which is what I checked rather than assumed:

- clients/reqwest.rs ships same_origin_redirect_policy, installed by new() / try_new(), comparing the preceding URL's origin to the target's and stopping otherwise. Note reqwest's own default follows up to 10 redirects to ANY origin, so this is an active override rather than a default inherited.
- clients/ureq.rs disables ureq's own redirect following entirely and implements the same-origin walk in fetch(), with GET following 301/302/303/307/308 and POST only 307/308 so the method and body survive.
- tests/review_reqwest_redirect.rs and tests/review_ureq_redirect.rs cover it, six tests, all passing. The cross-origin test mounts the internal mock with .expect(0) and calls verify(), so it asserts the internal server was NEVER CONTACTED rather than merely that the call returned an error -- the same rigour as pkix-aia-http/tests/async_ssrf.rs.

The asymmetry between the two crates' redirect handling is itself principled: aia-http refuses redirects outright because it applies its own destination policy and a redirect would escape it; revocation-http permits same-origin redirects because the caller's vetted origin is the boundary being preserved.

## What IS worth raising, and is filed separately

Two crates in one workspace have OPPOSITE defaults for the same threat. Both fetch URLs taken from a certificate whose signature has not been checked yet:

- pkix-aia-http: default-deny non-public destinations, with an opt-in escape hatch
- pkix-revocation-http: no destination policy, caller vets

Neither is wrong on its own terms, but a consumer who learns AIA fetching is SSRF-safe by default may reasonably assume revocation fetching is too, and nothing in either crate warns them. Filed as its own question rather than resolved here, because making them consistent is a design decision and not a bug fix.

## Acceptance

[x] Determined whether pkix-revocation-http's async backend applies a destination policy -- it does not, by explicit documented design
[x] IP literals: not applicable, since there is no filter to bypass. Recorded above rather than tested, because a test would assert nothing.
[x] The omission is documented at the trait boundary -- it already was, in the crate-level docs, and the same-origin redirect mitigation that makes it coherent is documented AND tested

{"id":"PKIX-eits","title":"pkix-ct: Google's CT log list signature is not verified","description":"## What

pkix-ct's CtLogList::from_google_log_list_json parses Google's log_list.json but does not verify Google's signature over it. Google publishes log_list.json alongside log_list.sig (a detached signature) and the public key that signs it, exactly as IANA publishes root-anchors.xml alongside root-anchors.p7s and the ICANN certificate.

This is the same provenance gap that pkix-dnssec-anchor closes for the DNSSEC root: the trust material is fetched from a URL and parsed on faith.

## Why it matters more here than for DNSSEC

The DNSSEC root KSK has rolled once since 2010. CT logs are added, frozen and retired continuously -- a consumer refreshes the log list on the order of weeks, not years. So the list is fetched often, by automation, from a network location, and every one of those fetches is currently unauthenticated. An attacker who can substitute the log list can add a log they control, and SCTs from it will then verify.

The CT log IDs are SHA-256 over the log's SPKI, so a substituted list cannot forge an SCT for an EXISTING log. The attack is adding an attacker-controlled log, which defeats the point of requiring SCTs at all.

## What is already right

pkix-ct does NOT bake in a log list. from_google_log_list_json takes a &str the caller supplies, and CtLogList::insert lets a caller build a list from any source. That matches the workspace rule that trust material is the caller's. What is missing is only the means to check that what the caller fetched is what Google published.

## Shape, following pkix-dnssec-anchor

The same split applies and is probably the right one:

- Verification of the signature belongs wherever the fetch happens -- which, since pkix-ct is no_std and does no I/O, means either a sibling adapter crate or a generator that runs at build/release time and commits a verified snapshot.
- A pkix-ct-loglist crate holding a signature-verified snapshot of the log list, versioned independently, is the direct analogue of pkix-dnssec-anchor. Given how often the list changes, a committed snapshot goes stale fast, so an adapter that fetches AND verifies at runtime may fit better here than the snapshot-in-a-crate shape that suits the DNSSEC root.

Decide which before building. The two have genuinely different update cadences and that is what should drive the choice.

## Also worth checking while in here

Whether Apple's log list (the other widely used one) is signed, and how. A consumer pinning only Google's list inherits Google's log-inclusion policy; the crate docs already note Apple and browser-specific lists as alternative sources.

## Acceptance

[ ] Decided: runtime-verifying adapter, committed verified snapshot, or both
[ ] Google's log_list.sig is verified against Google's published key before a list is trusted
[ ] A caller cannot accidentally use an unverified list without that being visible in the API

FIXED 2026-11-24. CtLogList::from_google_log_list_json_verified checks Google's detached signature before parsing anything. Eight tests against the real published artifacts; fmt / clippy / rustdoc -D warnings clean, 111 tests pass.

## Resolution of the open question this bead posed

The bead asked: runtime-verifying adapter, committed verified snapshot, or both -- and flagged that the choice should be driven by update cadence rather than copied from pkix-dnssec-anchor.

Answered by noticing the cadences point at DIFFERENT artifacts:

- the LOG LIST churns on the order of weeks, as logs are added, frozen and retired
- GOOGLE'S SIGNING KEY rotates rarely

So the thing worth pinning as data is the KEY, not the list -- the inverse of pkix-dnssec-anchor, where the anchor itself is the long-lived artifact. A committed snapshot of the list would go stale almost immediately and would push deployments back toward fetching it unverified.

Hence: a verifying constructor, with the key supplied by the caller and the list fetched at runtime. No new crate, no snapshot, and pkix-ct stays no_std with no network dependency. A pkix-ct-loglist crate shipping a snapshot was considered and rejected on cadence grounds.

## What was verified before writing code

The signature algorithm was confirmed rather than inferred. The 512-byte log_list.sig suggested RSA-4096, but the padding and digest were checked directly:

    openssl dgst -sha256 -verify log_list_pubkey.pem -signature log_list.sig log_list.json
    Verified OK

and a tampered copy was confirmed to fail. So: RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 with SHA-256 over the raw log_list.json bytes, key RSA-4096.

Also checked before designing: pkix-ct already depends on pkix-path, so SignatureVerifier was available and no new machinery was needed; and the trait's message parameter is documented as "DER-encoded TBSCertificate" but is in fact any byte slice, so it serves an arbitrary blob.

## Design decisions

- The algorithm is HARDCODED, not a parameter. Letting a caller choose would let anything able to influence that choice downgrade the check. A change on Google's side is a format change and should require a visible code change here.
- The key is a caller-supplied DER SubjectPublicKeyInfo. The crate ships none, consistent with shipping no log list and with pkix-path shipping no root certificates.
- Signature-related failures all map to the existing Error::InvalidSignature -- a bad signature, an unparseable key, an unsupported algorithm. Deliberately one variant: to a caller they all mean "do not trust this list", and splitting them would invite treating some as recoverable.
- Nothing is parsed until the signature verifies, so unverified garbage reports InvalidSignature rather than ParseError. Reporting a parse error would tell a caller the list was authentic but malformed.

## Testing against the real thing

tests/log_list_signature.rs uses Google's genuine published list, signature and key, committed with refresh instructions in tests/fixtures/REFRESH.md. A hand-rolled key and list would only prove the code is self-consistent; the property that matters is agreeing with what Google actually signs.

Negative cases: a byte flipped at three positions (start, middle, end -- a scheme noticing changes only near one end would pass a single-position test), an edit that leaves the JSON well-formed, a modified key with the DER header left intact so the failure is genuinely the signature check, malformed keys and signatures, and that nothing is parsed before verification.

The tests do not go stale as the list rotates: they assert the signature verifies and that tampering is caught, neither of which depends on the list being current. Rotation of the signing key would break them, which is rare and is exactly the kind of change worth being told about.

## Discoverability

from_google_log_list_json is unchanged and still exported -- a list reviewed and committed by hand needs no signature check. Its documentation now says plainly that it checks nothing and points at the verifying constructor, because a reader who finds the parsing function first would otherwise have no reason to look further.

## Also in this bead's scope, not done

Apple's log list. The bead asked whether it is signed and how. Not investigated: pkix-ct's docs already note Apple and browser-specific lists as alternative sources ingested through CtLogList::insert, and that path is unaffected by this change. Worth its own look if anyone pins Apple's list, since a consumer doing so inherits Apple's log-inclusion policy rather than Google's.

## Note on the earlier mis-close

This bead was closed in error on the same day with a reason belonging to the pkix-revocation-http destination-policy investigation, and reopened immediately. That reason should be disregarded; it is recorded on PKIX-xbhc, where it belongs.
